lessons.title: Barrier repair after over-use: a subtraction protocol and an honest recovery timeline
lessons.explanation: When a routine has been too aggressive, the skin does not need a better product; it needs fewer insults and time. Over-use presents as a cluster rather than a single symptom: stinging or burning within seconds of applying things that used to be comfortable, tightness that persists long after cleansing, visible flaking without a new product, and a spread of reactivity from one product to many. The repair logic follows the barrier model directly. Because the damage is a loss of intercellular lipid continuity and a disturbance of surface proteins and pH, the interventions that help are the ones that stop further loss and restore the components: stop the stripping and exfoliating steps, shorten and cool cleansing, apply a moisturiser with lipid and occlusive components to damp skin so water is held in rather than evaporating, and keep photoprotection because a permeable barrier takes more ultraviolet damage and irritation is itself a route to pigment change. Public-education material supports the practical elements: limit baths and showers to five to ten minutes in warm water, use a gentle cleanser sparingly and only where needed, pat rather than rub dry, and apply a fragrance-free moisturiser immediately after washing and again several times a day when skin feels dry. The timeline deserves honesty. Barrier recovery is a repair process measured in days to weeks for the symptoms and longer for the barrier to be fully restored, and it is easier to re-injure a recovering barrier than to injure a healthy one, which is why the temptation to resume actives early is the most common reason repair takes longer than it should. Three boundaries matter. Persistent problems that do not improve with subtraction are a clinical question, not a stronger moisturiser. If a learner has an existing condition such as atopic dermatitis, the repair plan is that condition's management with a clinician, and cosmetic steps sit inside that plan. And nothing here changes a prescribed treatment: the prescriber's instructions govern.
lessons.example: Worked example with a staged timeline and counted removal. A learner arrives with stinging, tightness and flaking after eight weeks of a routine containing a foaming cleanser twice daily, an exfoliating acid four times a week, a retinoid three nights a week, an alcohol toner daily and a fragranced serum. Start with subtraction arithmetic. Removing the exfoliating acid eliminates 32 applications in the next eight weeks; pausing the retinoid removes 24 applications; stopping the toner removes 56 applications. That is 112 permeability-increasing exposures removed from the next eight weeks by changing nothing except what is applied. Now stage the plan. Week one is subtraction only: a mild cleanser used once in the evening with a short, lukewarm wash, moisturiser applied generously to damp skin twice a day, photoprotection in the morning, nothing else, and no exfoliation or masks. Weeks two to four add discipline rather than products: hold the same routine and record three observations every Sunday, namely the duration of any stinging after cleansing, how long tightness lasts, and whether any site is flaking. Also write the rule that matters most: no active is reintroduced in this window, even if the skin feels better by the end of week two, because the feeling of recovery precedes the restoration of barrier function. Weeks four to eight are for a single planned reintroduction if, and only if, the observations have been stable for two consecutive weeks, using the trial design from lesson 42 with one variable, one window and a written stop rule. Note what the plan does not include: a new barrier-repair product added on top, which would leave the insulting steps in place and add a variable; and no resumption of the retinoid or the acid in the same month.
lessons.question: A learner's skin is stinging and flaking after two months of daily toner, four-times-weekly acid and three nights of retinoid. What is the defensible first move?
lessons.answer: Subtract the stripping and accelerating steps, moisturise damp skin generously, keep photoprotection, and reintroduce at most one active only after symptoms have been stable for two consecutive weeks
lessons.distractor: Add a ceramide-rich barrier repair cream and continue the existing steps, because repair ingredients can compensate for the ongoing irritation
lessons.correction: Repair ingredients can help restore lipids, but they cannot outrun continuing damage: the acid, toner and retinoid together remove far more barrier material per week than a cream restores. Subtracting those steps removes over a hundred permeability-increasing exposures in the next eight weeks, which is the intervention with the largest effect, and a stable fortnight is the precondition for testing anything new.

depth.definitions: Barrier repair is the restoration of stratum corneum lipid organisation, corneocyte cohesion and surface pH after damage. Occlusion is the use of a film-forming ingredient such as petrolatum to reduce transepidermal water loss, the outward flux of water vapour through the skin. Emollients are lipids that fill spaces between corneocytes and soften the surface. Applying to damp skin means applying within a short interval after washing, so that water held at the surface is trapped under the moisturising film rather than evaporating. Fragrance-free means the product contains no added fragrance or masking fragrance. Cumulative irritancy is the accumulation of sub-threshold damage from repeated exposure. A recovering barrier describes skin whose visible symptoms have resolved while its permeability and irritant thresholds have not yet returned to baseline. Atopic dermatitis is a chronic inflammatory skin disease, not a cosmetic dryness problem, and it is managed by a clinician.
depth.mechanism: Why subtraction works is a flux argument. Water crosses the stratum corneum along the intercellular lipid route, and when lamellar lipids are removed or disorganised, that route becomes more permeable, so water loss rises and applied substances reach live nerve endings more easily, which is felt as stinging. Intercellular lipids are not stored ready-made; the epidermis has to synthesise and organise them, and the corneocyte envelope and desmosome proteins have to be replaced, all of which takes time and requires that new damage stop. That is why the recovery curve has a shape: symptoms can improve quickly because inflammation settles first, while permeability and irritant thresholds lag, so the learner feels recovered before they are. Two mechanistic details explain the practical instructions. Applying moisturiser to damp skin changes what the film is trapping, since the water it holds is the water already on the surface; and occlusion works by reducing flux rather than by adding water, which is why a plain petrolatum-based product can help cracked, recently inflamed skin even though it contains no humectant. A limit belongs here too. The evidence base for many individual repair ingredients is thinner than the marketing implies, and reviews of the barrier note that much of what is known comes from models and controlled conditions; the reliable, well-supported parts of repair are subtracting insults, restoring lipids and water retention, and protecting from further damage. Nothing in this mechanism replaces clinical management of an active skin disease.
depth.secondExample: Contrasting application where the same presentation has a different history and therefore a different plan. Case one: a learner who used an unfamiliar acid on holiday two weeks ago, has no previous skin history, and now has stinging limited to the cheeks and a patch of flaking under one eye. Here the protocol above is proportionate, and the useful signs to track are whether the stinging duration after cleansing shortens week by week and whether the flaking area shrinks without spreading. Case two: a learner with lifelong itchy, dry, relapsing skin who started an acid at the same time as a seasonal flare. Subtracting the acid is right, but the framing is different: their flare is a disease exacerbation in a condition a clinician manages, and a cosmetic repair routine is adjunctive rather than decisive. Case three: hands rather than face. A person who washes their hands forty times a day for work has inflammation driven by repeated wetting and surfactant exposure, so the operative changes are gloves, hand-drying technique and leave-on emollients applied after every wash, not a facial routine transferred downward. Case four: symptoms that keep worsening despite subtraction for two weeks, or that include weeping, blistering, pus or pain. The mechanism is no longer the working hypothesis; the learner needs assessment. Same vocabulary of dry, stinging and flaking, four different indices of suspicion and four different actions.
depth.mistake: The characteristic error is treating repair as a product category: buying a 'barrier cream' while continuing the steps that caused the problem, which converts a subtraction task into an addition task and usually prolongs the episode. The second is early resumption, restarting the acid or retinoid the moment the skin feels normal, which lands the new exposure on a barrier whose permeability has not yet recovered. The third is interpreting improvement as permission to escalate: if a fortnight of gentle care produces softness, the response is to hold, not to add a second active. The fourth is the diagnostic shortcut, concluding from flushing and scaling that a learner 'has rosacea' or 'has eczema', when those determinations require clinical assessment and change the whole plan. Diagnose your own reasoning with three questions: which steps have I removed, and can I count the exposures that removal avoided? Have the three weekly observations been stable for two consecutive weeks before I test anything? And is there a red flag, such as pain, weeping, blistering, pus, fever, or a rash that spreads after stopping? If the answer to the third question is yes, the plan is clinical assessment rather than further adjustment, and if a clinician has prescribed a treatment, the repair plan must not quietly contradict it.
depth.application: Nonblocking task with a written observation sheet. Write your repair plan in three columns: what I stop (with the counted number of applications avoided over the next four weeks), what I keep (cleanser, moisturiser applied to damp skin, photoprotection), and what I observe each Sunday (stinging duration after cleansing, duration of tightness, whether any site flakes). Then write the reintroduction rule before you need it: the earliest week you may test one active, the evidence required to proceed, and the signs that would end the trial immediately. Model response: 'Stop: acid four times weekly, 16 applications avoided in four weeks; alcohol toner daily, 28 avoided; retinoid paused with my prescriber informed, 12 avoided. Keep: mild cleanser once at night, plain moisturiser to damp skin twice daily, broad-spectrum sunscreen each morning. Observe: stinging 90 seconds now, target under 15 by week four; tightness 20 minutes now; flaking on the chin only. Reintroduce: not before week five, only if weeks three and four are stable and identical, one product, stop rule for burning over a minute or any spread beyond the applied area.' Self-review rubric: (1) removals are counted, not merely listed; (2) the moisturiser is applied to damp skin and at a generous dose rather than a pea-sized dot; (3) the observation fields are visible and checkable; (4) the reintroduction rule is written in advance and names the signs that end the trial; (5) no prescribed treatment was stopped or changed without the prescriber, and there is a stated referral threshold for pain, weeping, blistering, pus, fever or a spreading rash, or a rash that has not improved after two weeks of gentle care.
depth.summary: Repair is subtraction plus time plus lipid and water restoration plus protection, in that order, with observation points that separate the fast resolution of symptoms from the slower restoration of permeability. Feelings of recovery arrive before recovery does, so the reintroduction rule is written before it is needed, and a recovering barrier earns one test at a time. Persistent, painful or relapsing problems leave cosmetic care and become clinical care, and any prescribed treatment stays exactly as the prescriber set it. With the routine stable and the barrier repaired, the next unit leaves the face to look at what the whole toolkit can and cannot do elsewhere on the body.

readings.title: National Institute of Arthritis and Musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases, Atopic Dermatitis (niams.nih.gov) — Overview and treatment overview sections
readings.note: Read the Overview for the description of atopic dermatitis as a chronic inflammatory disease with flares and remissions, that it is not contagious, and that genes, the immune system and the environment all play a role. Read the treatment overview for the role of moisturising and the statement that treatment can help control symptoms. Use it to keep two things distinct in your own notes: a cosmetic dry-skin episode after over-use, which this lesson covers, and a relapsing inflammatory disease, which needs a clinician and where cosmetic steps are adjunctive.

readings.title: American Academy of Dermatology, How to treat dry skin: Dermatologist tips for relief (aad.org) — the numbered tips
readings.note: Read tips 1 to 4 for the practical protocol used in this lesson: limit baths and showers to five to ten minutes in warm water and close the bathroom door, use a gentle cleanser sparingly and only where needed, shave at the end of washing, and apply a fragrance-free moisturiser immediately after patting dry and again several times a day. Tip 4 is the source of the damp-skin application and the repeated-use point.

readings.title: StatPearls, Moisturizers (NCBI Bookshelf) — Introduction, Function, and Issues of Concern
readings.note: Read for the definition of a moisturiser as a product intended to raise skin water content and restore barrier function, and for the description of the links between water content, corneodesmosomal connections and the appearance of dry, flaky skin below a critical water concentration. The Issues of Concern section is useful for the honest caveat that not every claim about a moisturising ingredient is equally supported. Bookshelf may show an automated-tool check; headings and abstract were retrievable by text extraction.

readings.title: Sensitive skin: review of an ascending concept (PMC5595600) — Predisponent factors, Environmental factors subsection
readings.note: Read the environmental factors subsection to see why recovery planning has to include more than products: cold, heat, sun, pollution and moisture all appear as triggers in the reviewed literature. Use it to justify why the repair protocol keeps photoprotection and shortens hot washing rather than only changing the routine's products.

visual.title: The repair curve: symptoms resolve before permeability does
visual.description: A timeline chart with weeks on the horizontal axis. A steep curve shows reported stinging and tightness falling within the first two weeks. A second, flatter curve shows barrier permeability and irritant threshold recovering over four to eight weeks, remaining below baseline while the first curve is already low. Below the chart, a three-column subtraction table counts avoided exposures, and a gate labelled reintroduction rule sits before the point where actives may resume.
steps: Week axis marked 0 to 8, with a shaded window labelled subtraction only for week one and hold steady for weeks two to four.
Curve 1: stinging duration and tightness falling steeply from day one to week two, labelled inflammation settles first.
Curve 2: permeability and irritant threshold rising slowly through weeks two to eight, labelled still below baseline while symptoms are already gone.
Gap annotation between the two curves: feeling recovered is not being recovered, which is why reintroduction is delayed.

Subtraction table: columns for step stopped, applications avoided over four weeks, and mechanism removed; rows for four-times-weekly acid (16), daily toner (28), paused retinoid (12), totalling 56 avoided applications in four weeks.

Gate before any reintroduction: stability for two consecutive weeks, one variable only, written stop rule for burning over a minute or spread beyond the applied area, plus a clinician review line for pain, weeping, blistering, pus, fever, or no improvement after two weeks.

questions.prompt: A learner's stable four-step routine is working and they add a fifth product that duplicates a job already covered, then a sixth to soothe the irritation the fifth caused. Using the routine audit, what is the correct reading and action?
questions.answer: The routine has accumulated duplicate jobs and a corrective addition, so the fifth and sixth steps should be removed to restore the tolerated baseline before any new decision
questions.distractor: The routine needed both steps, because soothing products mitigate irritation and a routine with more coverage is more thorough than one with less
questions.correction: A step earns its place by performing a job no other step performs. The fifth step repeats an existing job, so it adds exposure without adding function, and the sixth exists only to manage the consequence of the fifth, which is the corrective-addition pattern that raises total insult while solving nothing. Removing both restores the baseline that makes any later change interpretable.

questions.prompt: A learner starts a new cleanser, serum, moisturiser and sunscreen on the same day and develops an itchy rash on the cheeks and eyelids ten days later. They want to know which of the four is responsible. What does the attribution logic imply?
questions.answer: The observation cannot separate the candidates because four simultaneous introductions leave fifteen non-empty product combinations, so the exposure map and clinician assessment are needed rather than further guessing
questions.distractor: The cleanser is responsible because it contacts the skin longest, so removing it is the necessary and sufficient step
questions.correction: Four products started together produce fifteen possible explanations, four singles, six pairs, four triples and one set of four, and a visible rash does not discriminate among them. Eyelid involvement also points to transferred exposure, which may include a shampoo that was not among the four. Naming a substance is a diagnostic procedure for a clinician with the products available.

questions.prompt: A learner asks whether twenty percent niacinamide, twenty-five percent vitamin C and the strongest available azelaic acid should be used together nightly, on the grounds that stronger products must work better. Which response reflects the reported evidence?
questions.answer: The reported ranges sit lower, with niacinamide sebum findings around two to five percent and vitamin C above roughly eight percent gaining nothing above twenty, and azelaic products differ by formulation more than by percentage
questions.distractor: The percentages are fine because vitamin C needs to exceed twenty percent to be biologically active, and niacinamide at twenty percent is the standard strength for pigment problems
questions.correction: The reviews report sebum findings for niacinamide in the two to five percent range with tolerance documented to five and no stinging to ten, and vitamin C needing above about eight percent while adding nothing above twenty and possibly causing irritation. Azelaic acid's absorbed fraction differs sharply by vehicle, with the gel delivering far more of the dose into viable skin than the cream at a lower percentage, so percentage shopping across products is not a comparison. Three nightly actives also remove attribution.

questions.prompt: A learner uses a coarse scrub twice weekly, a glycolic acid toner twice weekly and an acid-containing weekly mask, and asks whether a finer scrub will resolve the flaring. What should the reasoning conclude?
questions.answer: Five exfoliating events per week act on one structure, so reduce to a single method at a single weekly event before substituting products, and expect pigment risk if irritation continues
questions.distractor: A finer scrub is the answer, because the flare is caused by particle abrasiveness rather than by the total number of exfoliating exposures reaching the stratum corneum
questions.correction: Mechanical and chemical exfoliation both accelerate desquamation and disturb the same surface structure, so gentler particles in one of five weekly events change little. Counting events and their spacing shows two pairs within 48 hours and 260 events a year. Because irritation is a documented route to post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, the expected outcome of continuing is new pigment rather than smoother texture.

questions.prompt: A learner presents with stinging, tightness and flaking after eight weeks of daily toner, four-times-weekly acid and three nights of a retinoid, and proposes to keep all steps but add a ceramide cream. Which plan is most consistent with the repair mechanism?
questions.answer: Pause the accelerating and stripping steps, cleanse briefly and gently, apply a plain moisturiser generously to damp skin twice daily, keep photoprotection, and allow two stable weeks before testing one active
questions.distractor: Keep every step and add the ceramide cream, because lipid replacement restores the intercellular lipids that the acid removed and therefore offsets the ongoing exposure
questions.correction: Lipid replacement helps, but it cannot outrun continuing removal: pausing those steps avoids dozens of permeability-increasing applications over the next four weeks, which is the larger effect. Symptoms settle before permeability recovers, so a stable fortnight is the precondition for testing anything, and the damp-skin application is what traps water rather than letting it evaporate. Any pain, weeping, blistering or lack of improvement after two weeks belongs with a clinician.

units.title: Beyond the face: scalp, body, daily sun, and accountable claim auditing

lessons.title: Scars and marks are not the same tissue: distinguishing redness, pigment, and textural change
lessons.explanation: After an inflamed lesion settles, three different things can remain, and they carry three different ceilings. Post-inflammatory erythema is redness from dilated microvessels left by wound healing, described in the scar literature as a wound-healing microvascular change that is perceived as general redness rather than visible broken vessels, and it is typically more persistent in fair skin. Post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation is excess melanin, usually brown, and is more typical in darker skin. A scar is a structural change: aberrant collagen production and degradation during healing, producing either a net loss of collagen in most cases or a net gain in others. The scar review reports that 80 to 90 percent of acne scars are atrophic from net collagen destruction, with the remainder hypertrophic or keloid from net gain, and it names the common atrophic types by shape and depth: icepick scars comprising about 60 to 70 percent, narrow tracts under two millimetres that reach the deep dermis; boxcar scars at about 20 to 30 percent, 1.5 to 4.0 millimetres wide with sharp vertical edges, shallow ones responding to resurfacing and deeper ones resisting it; and rolling scars at about 15 to 25 percent, the widest at up to five millimetres, created by fibrous anchoring of the dermis to the subcutis which produces an undulating surface. Those ranges overlap deliberately: they describe a mix seen in one person rather than a partition. The published expectation is blunt and worth repeating exactly: complete resolution of acne scarring is the exception rather than the rule. Public guidance from the American Academy of Dermatology says acne scars can fade but rarely go away completely on their own, recommends treating acne when it first appears to prevent scarring, and notes that having a close blood relative with acne scarring raises risk. This lesson is education about what kind of problem a learner is looking at, not a treatment plan, and procedures belong to clinicians.
lessons.example: Worked example that separates the three presentations and then sets an honest expectation. A learner presents with three features on the cheeks: uniform brown marks at the sites of old lesions, a few shallow oval depressions, and generalised redness that fades when the head is raised above heart level for a minute. Work through each. The brown marks are pigment: they sit in the epidermis if they are brown and relatively uniform, they fade by cell turnover over months, and the driver to remove first is any ongoing inflammation, because squeezing renews the pigment while the old mark clears. The shallow oval depressions with sharp edges are boxcar-type atrophic scars in the 0.1 to 0.5 millimetre range; the review reports that shallow boxcars are amenable to resurfacing while deeper ones at or beyond 0.5 millimetres resist it, which means the appropriate expectation for a topical routine is no change in the depression at all. The generalised redness is vascular, and the review notes that addressing erythema is the first step in a scar-management sequence because redness accentuates the appearance of textural change. Now do the distribution arithmetic to show why the categories must be read as a mix: the upper bounds of the reported ranges add to 125 percent and the lower bounds to 95 percent, which cannot be a partition of a single population and must instead describe coexisting types within individuals. That is why no learner should expect one scar type, one product or one procedure to address everything. The defensible plan states three separate goals: stop renewing the pigment by treating active acne under clinical guidance and not manipulating lesions; protect from ultraviolet exposure so pigment is not re-stimulated; and ask a clinician whether any of the textural component is treatable, while accepting that complete resolution is the exception rather than the rule.
lessons.question: A learner has flat brown marks, generalised redness, and several shallow oval depressions on the cheeks, and asks which serum will remove the depressions. Which answer reflects the evidence and the honest expectation?
lessons.answer: Textural change is a collagen defect rather than a surface pigmentation problem, so no topical routine removes it; pigmentation and vascular redness have their own slower timelines, and procedure options are a clinician's decision with complete resolution being the exception
lessons.distractor: The depressions are pigment sitting in a deeper layer, so a stronger lightening product applied for longer will lift them along with the flat brown marks
lessons.correction: Flat marks and depressions are different tissues. Brown marks are melanin that clears with epidermal turnover, redness is vascular, and depressions are net collagen loss or fibrous tethering of the dermis, which a topical product cannot rebuild or release. The scar literature reports that most acne scars are atrophic from collagen destruction and that complete resolution is the exception rather than the rule, which is why a topical plan should promise nothing about the depression and a clinician should be asked about the options that exist.

depth.definitions: Post-inflammatory erythema is persistent redness from microvascular dilatation after inflammation, without visible telangiectasia. Post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation is excess melanin deposited after inflammation, more common and often more severe in darker skin tones. An atrophic scar is a depression caused by net loss of dermal collagen; hypertrophic scars and keloids result from net collagen gain. Icepick scars are narrow tracts under two millimetres extending to deep dermis or subcutaneous tissue; boxcar scars are 1.5 to 4.0 millimetre oval depressions with sharply demarcated vertical edges, shallow at 0.1 to 0.5 millimetres and deep at or above 0.5; rolling scars are up to five millimetres wide and produced by fibrous anchoring of dermis to subcutis. Resurfacing describes procedures that remove controlled layers of skin. Expectation management means stating in advance what a given intervention can and cannot achieve. Skin phototype is a classification used to estimate pigmentary response.
depth.mechanism: The mechanism explains both the ceiling and the timeline. Pigment: inflammation stimulates melanocytes and increases transfer of melanosomes to keratinocytes, and because keratinocytes are shed on an approximately monthly cycle, an epidermal deposit clears only as those cells turn over, while melanin that reached the dermis has no shedding route. Redness: wound healing produces microvascular dilatation and, in the terms the scar review uses, repair-related epidermal thinning that makes the underlying vessels more visible, which is why the redness reduces when venous pressure falls and why it does not behave like pigment. Texture: healing that ends in a net loss of collagen leaves a volume deficit, and healing that anchors dermis to subcutis creates a tether that pulls the surface down, which explains why the appearance changes with facial movement and why topicals cannot change it. The scar literature also reports differences in the immune response between people who scar and those who do not, with infiltrates found in the majority of atrophic scars and a different early T-cell profile in people prone to scarring, which is why family history is treated as a risk marker rather than a coincidence. Two limits should be stated plainly: the ranges given for scar types describe what has been reported and used descriptively, and they are not a personal forecast; and nothing in this mechanism licenses a learner to classify their own lesions, because distinguishing a scar from a changing lesion is a clinical judgement with a much higher stake.
depth.secondExample: Contrasting cases that share the word 'mark' and require different handling. Case one: a learner with a fair phototype, several flat red patches at old lesion sites and no depressions. The working explanation is vascular, the plan is time plus control of active acne plus photoprotection, and the honest expectation is gradual fading. Case two: a learner with a darker phototype and brown patches of the same age. The explanation is pigment, the timeline is longer, and the risk that matters is that new irritation creates new pigment, so the plan emphasises not manipulating lesions and not exfoliating the marks aggressively. Case three: a learner with a family history of scarring acne, active deep lesions on the jaw, and the first shallow depressions appearing. The priority inverts: the cosmetic conversation about marks becomes secondary, and the clinical question about controlling the active disease is urgent because scarring is largely preventable and much less treatable once established. Case four: a learner with a raised, firm nodule at a healed site and a tendency to form raised scars elsewhere. That is a different scar type with a different risk profile and belongs with a clinician. Case five: a single new pigmented lesion that is asymmetric, enlarging, itching or bleeding, with no preceding inflammation. That is outside this lesson entirely and needs assessment. Five cases, five different first moves, and the distinguishing information is history and examination rather than the word the learner used.
depth.mistake: Three persistent errors. The first is treating all residual change as pigment and buying a product for it, which wastes months and can add irritation, since aggressive exfoliation of a mark is itself a way to create new pigment. The second is reading the presence of redness as evidence of active inflammation that needs more treatment, when vascular redness can persist long after the inflammation has resolved. The third is planning by aspiration rather than by tissue type: expecting a routine to produce a result that the tissue makes impossible, and then concluding the learner's skin is unusual. Diagnose by asking three questions of your own plan. Which component am I addressing: pigment, vessels, or collagen? What is this component's realistic route and timescale, given that pigment clears by turnover and collagen does not regenerate from a cream? And what is the referral trigger? Refer for painful or nodular active lesions, rapid worsening, any deep or already-established scarring, keloid-type or raised scars, family history of scarring acne with active deep lesions, or any new, changing, asymmetric, itching or bleeding pigmented lesion. Nothing in this lesson justifies treating active acne, scars or pigmentation with cosmetic products marketed as treatments, because those uses make a product a drug.
depth.application: Nonblocking task. Write a one-page residual-change inventory for one area of your face, in three columns: what I see, which tissue it most likely involves (pigment, vessels, or collagen), and what the honest route and timescale are according to the mechanism. Then add two lines: the referral decision, and one thing you will stop doing because it renews the driver. Model response: 'Cheek: flat brown patches, likely epidermal pigment, route is time plus controlling active acne plus photoprotection, timescale months; generalised redness, vascular, fades slowly, no product requirement; two shallow oval depressions, collagen loss, no topical route, clinical question only. Stop: squeezing new lesions, because it renews both pigment and inflammation. Referral: ask my clinician about the active acne and about whether the depressions are treatable, and see a clinician promptly for any new lesion that changes.' Self-review rubric: (1) each feature is assigned to a tissue type rather than to a product; (2) expectations are stated in months or as not achievable, not in weeks; (3) a stop-doing item addresses the driver; (4) referral triggers are written out, including any changing lesion; (5) no procedure is self-administered and no prescription is altered. Recheck the inventory in twelve weeks with a same-condition photograph and note whether the driver was ever fully stopped.
depth.summary: Pigment, vessels and collagen produce three different leftovers with three different ceilings: melanin clears with turnover, redness resolves on its own schedule, and textural change is a structural defect that topicals cannot rebuild. The scar literature's own words set the expectation, which is that complete resolution is the exception rather than the rule, and the strongest lever available to a learner is prevention through treating active acne early and not manipulating lesions. With honest expectations on the face, the next lesson moves to the site where routine mistakes are most often misdiagnosed: the scalp and hair.

readings.title: Acne Scarring — Pathogenesis, Evaluation, and Treatment Options (PMC5749614) — PATHOGENESIS, EVALUATION and the opening of TREATMENT
readings.note: Read PATHOGENESIS for the distinction between post-inflammatory erythema as wound-healing microvascular dilatation and post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation as more typical in dark skin, then for the 80 to 90 percent atrophic figure, and for the reported scar-type ranges: icepick about 60 to 70 percent, boxcar about 20 to 30 percent at 1.5 to 4.0 millimetres, and rolling about 15 to 25 percent up to five millimetres. Read EVALUATION for the expectation-management paragraph containing the statement that complete resolution of acne scarring is the exception rather than the rule. Read the treatment section only for orientation; the procedures described are clinician-delivered.

readings.title: American Academy of Dermatology, Acne scars (aad.org) — 'Are acne scars permanent?' and 'Can you prevent acne scars?'
readings.note: Read the patient-facing statement that acne scars can fade but rarely go away completely on their own, and the prevention section, which says treating acne when it first appears can prevent scars and that having a close blood relative with acne scarring raises risk. Use it when a learner asks whether patience alone will resolve a depression, and note the referral line to a board-certified dermatologist rather than any product recommendation.

readings.title: National Institute of Arthritis and Musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases, Acne (niams.nih.gov) — causes and treatment overview
readings.note: Read the plain-language description of what makes acne more likely and the reminder that improvement takes time. It supports the causal order this lesson insists on: residual change of any type is downstream of inflammation, so the driver has to stop before any expectation about fading or treatment is meaningful. Health information for the public; treatment decisions belong with a clinician.

visual.title: Three leftovers, three tissues, three ceilings
visual.description: A skin cross-section with three labelled residual features after an old lesion: dilated vessels producing redness, melanin granules held within keratinocytes producing a brown mark, and a collagen deficit producing a depression. Each is connected to a ceiling box stating its route and timescale, and a fourth box shows a raised firm scar with a referral arrow. A prevalence strip shows the reported scar-type ranges with an explicit note that they overlap.
steps: Cross-section: epidermis above dermis, with a healed lesion site marked at the surface.

Feature 1: dilated microvessels in the upper dermis drawn as widened vessels, labelled post-inflammatory erythema, with a note that reducing venous pressure makes the colour fade and that it persists longer in fair skin.

Feature 2: melanin transfer from a melanocyte to keratinocytes, labelled pigment with an epidermal turnover route measured in months, and a second branch showing dermal pigment with no shedding route.
Feature 3: a collagen deficit drawn as a volume gap with fibrous strands tethering dermis to subcutis, labelled textural change with the caption no topical route, clinical options only.
Feature 4: a raised firm nodule labelled hypertrophic or keloid scarring, with an arrow to clinical assessment.

Prevalence strip: icepick 60 to 70 percent, boxcar 20 to 30 percent, rolling 15 to 25 percent, with an annotation showing the upper bounds summing to 125 percent and the explanation that types coexist within one person.

Expectation banner across the bottom: the quoted finding that complete resolution of acne scarring is the exception rather than the rule, beside a prevention arrow pointing back to treating active acne early.

lessons.title: Scalp and hair: the same barrier with different exposure, and why hair damage is mostly cumulative
lessons.explanation: The scalp is skin, with the same stratum corneum, the same susceptibility to surfactant damage and the same capacity to react to allergens, but it is exposed differently: it is washed with products designed for the hair shaft as well as the scalp, it is occluded by hair, and it is frequently the site where a learner cannot easily see what is happening. The hair shaft itself is a different material. Its outer cuticle is covered by a covalently bound fatty acid layer, described in hair-cosmetics literature as the 18-MEA lipid layer, whose removal renders the fibre hydrophilic. Hair is porous and damaged hair is intensely so, and water absorption swells the shaft. The review gives the mechanical figures that explain why handling matters more than most products: when wet, undamaged hair can be stretched by about 30 percent of its original length without damage, irreversible change occurs between about 30 and 70 percent, and stretching to 80 percent causes fracture. Damage accumulates through a process the literature calls weathering, the progressive degeneration from root to tip, driven by daily grooming, chemical treatment and environmental exposure, visible microscopically as cuticle scaling, loss of the 18-MEA layer and cuticle cracking; if the cuticle is removed, the cortex is exposed and fibre fracture can follow. Shampoos are a surfactant system, with 10 to 30 ingredients typically, grouped into cleansing agents, additives, conditioning agents and special-care ingredients, and the review notes that although shampoos are considered safe, they can cause contact dermatitis, naming common allergens that include cocamidopropyl betaine, methylchloroisothiazolinone, formaldehyde-releasing preservatives, propylene glycol, tocopherol, parabens and benzophenones. That list matters because a scalp or hairline reaction is usually a clinical question about a product exposure, not a sign that the learner has washed badly. This lesson is education, not diagnosis.
lessons.example: Worked example with an exposure map and a handling audit. A learner reports scalp itching with flaking and a red, itchy rash at the hairline and behind the ears, and has recently changed shampoo, added a leave-in treatment and started using a weekly scalp scrub. Map the exposures rather than the symptoms: shampoo, leave-in treatment and scalp scrub all contact the scalp margin, and the leave-in stays on the skin rather than being rinsed, which raises both the concentration and the contact time at exactly the site that is symptomatic. Now add the transfer logic from lesson 42: a rinse-off product that runs down the face at night can affect the eyelid, and a product applied with the hands can reach the ears and neck. Then apply the allergen list: several of the named allergenic substances are preservatives and surfactants found in ordinary shampoos, so 'it is just shampoo' is not an exclusion. The handling audit follows a different logic, because mechanical damage is cumulative: count the aggressive events. Daily towel rubbing of wet hair, brushing wet hair from the roots down, and a daily hot-iron session at one pass over the same section add up to roughly 30 tugging or heating events a week, and the review's stretch data explain why wet hair is the worst time to apply force. The corrected version is not a new product but a different sequence: shampoo the scalp rather than the length, let the rinse water carry product down the shaft, condition after every wash, wrap rather than rub to remove water, and comb from the ends upward once the hair is partially dry. Both parts of the plan are single-variable measures with defined observations: the scalp margin is photographed weekly for the reaction, and breakage is counted as the number of short broken hairs visible on the pillow or in the brush.
lessons.question: A learner with scalp itching, hairline rash and frequent breakage asks whether a stronger anti-dandruff shampoo or a protein treatment is the better next purchase. What is the more defensible reading?
lessons.answer: The rash is a product-exposure question that needs clinical assessment with the products available, while breakage is cumulative mechanical and chemical damage, so the next step is a handling audit and an exposure map rather than another product
lessons.distractor: A stronger medicated shampoo is the better purchase, because scalp flaking proves a hygiene or fungal problem, and protein treatments repair the breakage at the same time
lessons.correction: Scalp scaling and itching have several possible causes and cannot be assigned from the grocery aisle, and hairline and eyelid involvement points to a contact reaction rather than to poor hygiene. Meanwhile breakage follows cumulative weathering and mechanical stress, which the stretch data explain: wet hair tolerates roughly 30 percent extension, with irreversible change above that and fracture near 80 percent. Neither problem is answered by escalating products, and naming a cause is a clinician's job.

depth.definitions: The hair shaft consists of a cuticle, a cortex and, in some fibres, a medulla; the cuticle is the protective outer layer. The 18-MEA layer is a covalently bound fatty acid on the fibre surface that makes hair hydrophobic, and its removal makes hair hydrophilic. Weathering is the progressive degeneration of the fibre from root to tip. A shampoo is a surfactant-based cleansing system, and surfactants are classified as anionic, cationic, amphoteric and non-ionic. A conditioner is a formulation intended to reduce friction, improve combability and reduce water uptake, often using cationic surfactants and silicones that deposit on the fibre. Traction alopecia is hair loss caused by sustained pulling from tight hairstyles. Seborrheic dermatitis is an inflammatory scalp and skin condition that a clinician diagnoses; dandruff is a lay term for visible scalp scaling. Contact dermatitis is an inflammatory reaction to an irritant or allergen, divided into irritant and allergic forms.
depth.mechanism: Two mechanisms operate at once, and the distinction explains why products and technique get separate attention. At the fibre, damage is sequential. Grooming and chemical treatment lift cuticle scales and remove the 18-MEA layer, water then enters more readily and swells the shaft, and with the cortex exposed, further friction or heat produces fracture, which is why damaged hair breaks rather than stretches. Thermal treatment adds a chemistry problem: the literature describes decomposition of tryptophan residues into kynurenine-type oxidation products, associated with yellowing of white hair and darkening of bleached hair, and notes that a lipid-rich product can temporarily restore combability while the underlying heat damage remains after the next wash. At the scalp, the mechanism is the barrier story from the first unit of this level with a different exposure pattern: surfactants remove intercellular lipids, allergens penetrate more easily on a compromised surface, and occlusion by hair plus warm water raises the effective exposure. The review reports that a hair dryer held about 15 centimetres away and kept moving caused less damage than natural drying in the work it cites, which is a good example of a counterintuitive finding that should be reported as the cited study's result rather than as a general rule, because technique and distance are doing the work. What no mechanism here supports is the idea that a scalp product can 'feed' the follicle or that oiling stimulates growth; hair is a dead keratin structure once it leaves the follicle, and growth is governed below the surface.
depth.secondExample: Contrasting application where fibre geometry and chemistry change the plan. Consider a learner with tightly curled hair and a scalp that reacts easily. The review describes variation in fibre diameter along the length, a twisted or ellipsoidal cross section, lower water content, and torsions along the thread compared with straighter hair, which means that detangling force distributes unevenly and that a single broken point can travel. The same review describes chemical straightening chemistry, including hydroxide-based relaxers that work by lanthionisation and thioglycolate-based alternatives that selectively weaken cystine bonds before being oxidised and neutralised, with the cited finding that a no-lye relaxer was less irritating to the scalp than a lye relaxer and the authors' recommendation that people with very curly hair and sensitive scalps use no-lye products. Now change the learner rather than the fibre: a swimmer whose hair is exposed to pool chemicals repeatedly, where the published advice is to wear a swim cap, rinse immediately, and use a swimmers' shampoo followed by deep conditioning. Now change the site: a scalp that flakes but does not itch or react, in a person taking other topical treatments. Here the question is whether the scaling is a treatable condition or the ordinary consequence of a product, which is a judgement for a clinician rather than a shopping decision. Same subject area, three sets of constraints, none answerable by comparing brand claims.
depth.mistake: Four errors recur. The first is hygiene moralising: reading scalp scaling and itching as proof of inadequate washing and escalating to harsher products, when the same scaling can come from a treatable inflammatory condition, an irritating product, or a learned risk that more washing aggravates. The second is the growth myth, believing scalp oils, massage or 'stimulating' shampoos grow hair, when the follicle's activity is not governed by surface products and hair loss needs assessment. The third is handling blindness, focusing entirely on what is bought and ignoring the mechanical events that accumulate: wet brushing, towel rubbing, heat, and tight styles that pull continuously. The fourth is single-timepoint diagnosis, deciding which product caused a scalp reaction from appearance alone, when the pattern, the timing and the exposure map are what a clinician uses. Diagnose your own reasoning with three questions: what did I change, when, and does the pattern match an irritant response, a delayed reaction, or a cumulative one? What force and heat have I applied to wet hair this week, counted as events? And is the symptom in the domain of cosmetic care at all, or does it involve hair loss, a persistent itchy rash, bleeding, painful scalp lesions, or scaling that continues despite simplification? Those are clinical questions, and hair loss in particular should be assessed rather than treated from packaging.
depth.application: Nonblocking task with two records. Record one: a seven-day handling log counting events — days with wet brushing, towel rubbing, heat-tool passes, tight styles worn, and chemical treatments within the last eight weeks. Then compute the weekly total of tugging and heating events. Record two: an exposure list for everything contacting the scalp and hairline, including shampoo, conditioner, leave-in, dry shampoo, hair oil, hair dye, and any styling product, each with the date it was first used and whether it is rinsed off or left on. Model response: 'Handling: wet brushing 7, towel rubbing 7, heat 7 sessions at about 4 passes, tight ponytail 5 days, colour 3 weeks ago, weekly total about 50 tugging or heating events. Exposures: new leave-in started 12 days ago, left on, applied at the hairline; new shampoo 12 days ago. Observation: itchy rash began 9 days ago at the hairline and behind the ears, so both new products are suspects and the leave-on has the longer contact time.' Self-review rubric: (1) handling events are counted rather than described; (2) the exposure list separates rinse-off from leave-on and includes dates; (3) the plan changes one handling habit at a time and one product at a time, with a defined window; (4) referral triggers are written down, covering scalp rash that persists or spreads, painful or bleeding scalp lesions, sudden or patchy hair loss, and scaling that does not improve after simplification; (5) no medicated or prescription scalp product is started, stopped or altered without a clinician, and no dye or relaxer is reapplied to an irritated scalp.
depth.summary: The scalp is skin under a different exposure pattern, while the hair shaft is a dead keratin structure whose damage accumulates through cuticle loss, 18-MEA removal, water uptake and mechanical or thermal stress, with the practical figures being roughly 30 percent reversible wet stretch, irreversible change above that, and fracture near 80. Shampoos are surfactant systems that can also cause contact dermatitis, which makes a scalp or hairline reaction an assessment question rather than a hygiene verdict, and hair loss is never a product-selection problem. Count the handling events, map the exposures, change one thing at a time. The next lesson takes the same discipline to larger, harder-working surfaces: the body and the hands.

lessons.title: Body and hand care for dry or reactive skin: dose, wet work, and site-specific vehicles
lessons.explanation: The body is not the face at a larger size, and the hands are not the forearms. Three site properties change the arithmetic and the plan. Body surface area is large, so the amount of product needed to reach an adequate dose is an order of magnitude beyond face care, which makes concentration and cost per use central rather than incidental. Sebaceous glands are sparse on the limbs and the skin there often has fewer lipids available, so water loss and roughness are more common than oiliness, and the surface tolerates richer vehicles that the face would reject. And the hands occupy a special position: they are washed many times a day, they are exposed to surfactants and solvents, they are occluded by gloves, and they must keep working. The occupational literature is clear about what this means. Contact dermatitis is the most common occupational skin disease, making up around 80 percent of occupational skin diseases, and irritant contact dermatitis accounts for roughly half to four-fifths of those cases; the mechanism for the irritant form is damage to the skin barrier. Occupations with higher incidence in the reviewed data include healthcare, hairdressing, food preparation, cleaning-related work, painting and agriculture. Wet work, defined in that literature as activities where the skin is in contact with water and other liquids for extended periods, is repeatedly identified as a main risk factor, which is why the practical intervention is not a stronger cream but a change in how the hands get wet and dry. Public guidance on dry skin maps onto this directly: short warm showers rather than long hot ones, gentle cleanser used sparingly and only where needed, patting rather than rubbing dry, and moisturiser applied immediately after washing and again several times a day. This lesson is education about dose, site and exposure, not a treatment for hand eczema, which is a clinical condition.
lessons.example: Worked example that combines dose arithmetic with an exposure count. A learner with dry, cracked hands wants to know how much moisturiser to buy for a winter. Compute the area first. Using the standard burn-assessment approximation that one hand including the fingers is about one percent of total body surface area, two hands are about two percent; with total body surface area taken as 1.8 square metres, or 18,000 square centimetres, two hands come to about 360 square centimetres. At the tested benchmark dose of 2 milligrams per square centimetre, each application needs 360 multiplied by 2, which is 720 milligrams, or 0.72 grams. Applied twice daily for twelve weeks, that is 0.72 times 2 times 84, which is about 121 grams. So a 100-gram tube does not cover a single winter at an adequate dose, and a learner who buys a small facial-sized product will run out in three weeks and conclude that moisturiser does not work, when in fact the dose was never sustainable. Now do the exposure count. If the learner washes their hands eight times on a workday and three times on each weekend day, that is 40 plus 6, so 46 washes a week, roughly 2,400 a year, each one a surfactant exposure followed by a drying period. Glove use adds occlusion, which paradoxically can worsen maceration if gloves are worn wet for hours, and the occupational literature lists wet work as a main risk factor. The corrected plan therefore has three components, each with its own arithmetic: after every wash, pat dry and apply a leave-on emollient, which is the same 0.72 grams per application; reduce the number of unnecessary washes and the duration of water contact; and choose gloves by task, with appropriate drying time between wearing periods. Note what the plan does not include: a prescription topical, which is the clinician's decision, and any assumption that hand redness is only dryness, since persistent hand dermatitis is a clinical condition.
lessons.question: Using the test dose of 2 milligrams per square centimetre, roughly how much moisturiser does a learner need for two hands of about 360 square centimetres applied twice daily for twelve weeks?
lessons.answer: About 0.72 grams per application and roughly 121 grams across the twelve weeks, so a 100-gram tube does not cover a winter at an adequate dose
lessons.distractor: About 7.2 grams per application and roughly 1,210 grams across the twelve weeks, which is why a single tube of hand cream is always inadequate
lessons.correction: Multiply area by dose: 360 square centimetres times 2 milligrams per square centimetre is 720 milligrams, which is 0.72 grams, and 0.72 grams twice daily for 84 days is about 121 grams. The distractor is a factor of ten out because it skips the milligram-to-gram conversion; the conclusion that a 100-gram tube is insufficient still holds, but for the correct reason.

depth.definitions: Body surface area is the total area of the skin, conventionally estimated with rules such as the rule of nines, in which each entire arm is about 9 percent, each leg about 18 percent, and the head and neck about 9 percent; the palm excluding fingers is about 0.5 percent and a whole hand including fingers about 1 percent. The tested dose of 2 milligrams per square centimetre is the same benchmark used in sunscreen and barrier-product measurement. Wet work is occupational contact with water and liquids for extended periods. Irritant contact dermatitis is direct barrier damage from chemical or physical exposure without an immune mechanism; allergic contact dermatitis is a delayed hypersensitivity reaction. A leave-on emollient is a moisturising product applied and left in place, as distinct from a rinse-off cleanser. Maceration is skin softening and breakdown from prolonged moisture, which is a reason that glove use requires attention to drying. Hand eczema is a clinical condition that may be irritant, allergic or endogenous, and it is diagnosed and managed by a clinician.
depth.mechanism: Start with why the hands are the hardest-working site. Their stratum corneum is thicker than the face's, but they are washed far more often, and each wash is a two-part insult: surfactants extract intercellular lipids and bind surface proteins, and the water itself removes water-soluble natural moisturising factor and swells and then dries the tissue. Repeated wetting and drying cycles are more damaging than one long soak because each drying phase draws water out and leaves the surface slightly more permeable, and the reviewed occupational data identify cumulative wet work as a main risk factor for hand dermatitis. Then add the occlusion problem: a glove worn over damp or wet skin traps moisture, softens the stratum corneum and raises its permeability, so gloves can amplify exposure to whatever is inside them, which is why glove selection, wearing duration and drying between periods matter as much as the glove material. Then the lipid argument for the rest of the body: on the limbs, fewer sebaceous glands and, in older skin, slower barrier lipid synthesis mean less surface lipid is available, so fine oils, scales and itch appear, and the efficacious step is to supply lipids and reduce water loss rather than to add water. That is the mechanism behind the public advice to apply moisturiser to damp skin several times a day rather than once, and behind the site argument for richer vehicles on the body. The limit to state honestly is that this mechanism describes ordinary dry skin; it does not explain or manage a persistent hand rash with vesicles, cracking and pain, which needs assessment and may have an allergic component that only patch testing can identify.
depth.secondExample: Contrasting applications where the site decides the vehicle rather than the severity. A learner whose shins crack and itch every winter: the tissue is thick, lipid-poor and under mechanical load, so a heavy occlusive-rich product at a generous dose twice daily is appropriate, and the arithmetic above applies to the legs with a much larger area, so a 400-gram tub is a reasonable purchase rather than an indulgence. Now change the site to the underarms or groin: the same heavy product that succeeds on the shins is a poor choice in flexures, where occlusion traps heat and moisture and maceration is the predictable cost, so a lighter emollient-rich preparation belongs there. Now change the person: a healthcare worker who performs hand hygiene dozens of times per shift and cannot reduce the wetting. Here the intervention is sequencing and product form, not intensity, and the reviewed occupational literature's emphasis on wet-work exposure is what directs it: dry hands thoroughly, use a leave-on emollient after every wash if possible and at minimum at each break, avoid rings that trap moisture and residue, and use gloves for wet tasks rather than for long stretches of dry work. Now change the presentation: a learner with a persistent itchy, cracked hand rash that has not improved after two weeks of consistent emollient use. That is not an emollient failure; it is a clinical presentation, and appropriate assessment should precede any further product experimentation, particularly since an allergic component would change the plan entirely.
depth.mistake: Four errors. The first is facial dosing on a large surface: a pea-sized amount for both hands or both shins, which leaves the vehicle too thin to act and produces the false conclusion that the product does not work. The second is buying by elegance rather than by dose economics, choosing a small, expensive, pleasant product for a large-area problem and then rationing it. The third is washing more because it feels soothing in the moment, which adds surfactant and water exposure to an already dried surface; the reviewed data's emphasis on wet work is the correction. The fourth is assuming hand redness and cracking must be simple dryness, when hand dermatitis has irritant, allergic and endogenous forms, and the appearance does not separate them. Diagnose your own plan with three questions. Have I computed the amount needed for the area, at the same benchmark dose used for tested products? Do my teeth-gritting moments involve water contact, and can any of them be moved to another person, another tool, or another time? And is there anything here that a clinician should see, such as persistent cracking, vesicles, bleeding, pain, or a rash that does not improve after two weeks of consistent, fragrance-free emollient use? Refer also if the hands are affecting work, if there is severe itching at night, if the rash keeps spreading after you have stopped the likely exposures, or if a learner is considering a medicated or prescription topical, which requires clinician direction rather than improvisation.
depth.application: Nonblocking task with arithmetic. Run a two-part calculation for the site you actually care about. Part one: estimate the area in square centimetres (use about 360 for two hands, about 1,000 for a forearm pair if you cover that much, and the rule-of-nines fractions of 18,000 for larger areas), then compute grams per application at 2 milligrams per square centimetre, then multiply by applications per day and days per month. Part two: count your weekly water exposures for that site, including hand washes, showers, dishwashing and glove hours. Then write the three changes you will make. Model response: 'Two hands, 360 square centimetres, so 0.72 grams per application; twice daily is 1.44 grams a day, about 44 grams a month, so a 150-gram tub covers about three and a half months. My weekly water exposures: 46 hand washes plus dishwashing about 5 times plus glove hours about 20. Changes: leave-on emollient after every wash, gloves only for wet tasks and removed for drying, and a pump dispenser at the sink so the dose is easy.' Self-review rubric: (1) area, dose and unit conversions are shown; (2) the assumption about which surface area you are covering is stated; (3) the product is fragrance-free and applied to skin patted dry, not rubbed; (4) three changes are named, at least one of which reduces water contact rather than adding product; (5) no prescription topical is started or altered, and there is a written referral threshold for persistent cracking, vesicles, bleeding, pain, night itching, work impact, or a rash that keeps spreading despite removing likely exposures.
depth.summary: Site determines vehicle and dose determines effect: the body needs far more product per application than the face, the limbs need lipids rather than water because their surface film is thin, and the hands are dominated by the arithmetic of wet work and glove occlusion. Occupational data identify contact dermatitis as the most common occupational skin disease and wet work as a main risk factor, which is why the interventions that matter reduce water contact and supply lipids after every wash rather than escalating product strength. Persistent hand problems are clinical presentations, not dry-skin failures. The next lesson applies the same practical reasoning to the one measure that protects every one of these sites: sun protection in ordinary days rather than on holiday.
