lessons.title: Sun protection for ordinary days: incidental exposure, missed surfaces, and habits that beat intensity
lessons.explanation: Most ultraviolet exposure does not happen on a beach. It accumulates in fifteen-minute walks, in the driver's seat, at a desk by glass, on a lunch break, and through winter days that feel harmless. That makes the design problem different from holiday protection: the goal is a habit that survives an ordinary week rather than a maximum applied twice a year. Published guidance converges on three measures used together rather than one used alone. The American Academy of Dermatology recommends seeking shade, remembering that the sun's rays are strongest between 10 a.m. and 2 p.m., and using a simple test that anyone can apply anywhere: if your shadow is shorter than you are, seek shade. It recommends sun-protective clothing, including a lightweight long-sleeved shirt, pants, a wide-brimmed hat and sunglasses, and notes that clothing carrying an ultraviolet protection factor number offers more effective protection than fabric alone. It also recommends sunscreen, and for winter the same guidance applies with specific product directions: broad-spectrum, water-resistant, SPF 30 or higher, applied at least fifteen minutes before exposure and reapplied at least every two hours or after swimming or sweating, with the reminder not to overlook the ears, nose, lips, back of the neck, and the tops of the hands and feet. The arithmetic of a habit explains why the ordinary days dominate. A twenty-minute average daily outdoor exposure, five days a week for a year, is about 65 hours. A two-week holiday at two hours a day outdoors is 28 hours. The commuting pattern delivers more than twice the exposure hours of the holiday, with the important difference that it is incidental, easily ignored, and unaccompanied by any plan, while the holiday is planned and protected. Add the spectral point from the earlier level: ultraviolet A passes through window glass far more readily than ultraviolet B, is present year-round, and produces no burn, so the desk by the window does not announce itself. This lesson is education about exposure design, not a personal risk calculation, and any concern about an existing skin lesion is a clinical question.
lessons.example: Worked example that designs a normal week rather than a holiday. A learner describes four repeated exposures: a fifteen-minute walk to transport each weekday, a two-hour drive home with sun through the side window in the late afternoon, a desk beside a window for six hours, and a weekend run of about forty minutes. Compute the weekly hours: the walks are 15 minutes times 2 times 5, which is 2.5 hours; the drive is 10 hours; the desk is 30 hours by the window; the run is about 40 minutes. The desk hours are not full-intensity sun exposure, but the glass transmits ultraviolet A, which is exactly the component that does not produce a warning signal, so the design question is what a habit can do rather than what an application can cover. Now build three layers. Layer one is environmental: move the desk so the sunny side is behind the learner, close a blind during the strongest hours, or use shade for the walk, which costs nothing and cannot be forgotten. Layer two is clothing: a hat with a brim for the walk and the run, sunglasses with ultraviolet protection, and a long-sleeved light layer for the drive; clothing protection does not need reapplying or remembering at 2 p.m. Layer three is sunscreen, applied to the face, ears, neck, lips and the backs of the hands at about 1.2 grams for a 600-square-centimetre face-and-neck area, at least fifteen minutes before the walk, and reapplied when the learner will be outdoors for more than two hours or after sweating. Then run the dose arithmetic for a long outdoor day: eight hours outdoors with reapplication every two hours means the initial application plus four reapplications, so five applications, which for the face, ears and neck at about 1.8 grams each is roughly 9 grams, plus a body dose at 36 grams per full application if skin is exposed. That is why the design prioritises the cheap, forgettable layers first and reserves sunscreen for uncovered skin, rather than treating one product as the whole plan.
lessons.question: A learner wears a broad-spectrum SPF 50 sunscreen once each morning and reports no sunburn, while driving two hours daily with sun through the side window and sitting six hours by glass. What does the photobiology and dose logic say about their protection?
lessons.answer: The absence of burning says nothing about the ultraviolet A dose received through glass, and a single morning application is not maintained through a two-hour drive, so the effective gains are shade, clothing and reapplication rather than a higher printed factor
lessons.distractor: The absence of burning proves the sunscreen is working as labelled, so the current approach is sufficient and only the factor needs to be raised on holiday
lessons.correction: Erythema is a predominantly ultraviolet B response, and window glass attenuates ultraviolet B far more than ultraviolet A, so a long, unburning exposure can still deliver meaningful ultraviolet A. The labelled value also assumes the tested dose of 2 milligrams per square centimetre, while a morning application applied once and worn through a drive and a working day is not at that dose by mid-afternoon. Reapplication and non-product measures address the deficit; a higher number on the same bottle does not.

depth.definitions: The sun protection factor is a ratio of the ultraviolet dose needed to produce erythema on protected skin to that on unprotected skin, measured at 2 milligrams per square centimetre. Broad spectrum is a label claim permitted when a product passes a defined test showing that ultraviolet A protection is proportional to ultraviolet B protection. Water resistance is a bounded, measured label claim in minutes; waterproof and sweatproof are not permitted claims. Ultraviolet protection factor is the clothing equivalent, describing how much ultraviolet radiation passes through fabric. The ultraviolet index is an erythema-weighted forecast that tracks burning risk rather than total exposure. Incidental exposure is ordinary exposure during daily activity, as distinct from intentional sunbathing. The shadow rule is the practical estimate that when your shadow is shorter than you are, the sun is high and shade is advisable. Photoprotection refers to protecting skin from ultraviolet and visible radiation by any combination of shade, clothing, sunglasses and sunscreen.
depth.mechanism: Three mechanisms explain the design order. First, protection is cumulative and imperfect: no product blocks all ultraviolet radiation, and even a broadly protective routine leaves some dose, which means reducing exposure is always part of the answer rather than a substitute for product. Sunscreen absorbs or scatters photons in a film whose effectiveness depends on the amount present in the light path, so delivered protection falls when the applied amount falls below the tested 2 milligrams per square centimetre, which is why real-world application rates of roughly 0.5 to 1.5 milligrams per square centimetre are described in the literature and why reapplication matters more than a marginally higher factor. Second, transmission differs by wavelength and material: glass and clothing attenuate ultraviolet B far more than ultraviolet A, and reflection from snow, sand and water increases the dose arriving at the skin from below, which is why winter sports and water sports raise exposure rather than lowering it. Third, the biology distinguishes the ranges: ultraviolet B is absorbed directly by DNA and produces erythema within hours, while ultraviolet A penetrates deeper and works largely through reactive oxygen species, producing pigment change, photoaging and immunosuppression without a warning signal. That asymmetry is the reason this lesson builds a habit around shade, clothing and reapplication rather than around a single number, and it is also why the learner's own experience of not burning should be treated as an absence of data rather than as evidence of protection. One limitation to state: the literature on visible light and pigmentation, and on vitamin D synthesis, involves real clinical questions, and if a learner is concerned about either, that is a conversation with a clinician rather than something to resolve by adjusting a sunscreen routine.
depth.secondExample: Contrasting applications where the same three-layer framework produces different priorities. Case one: an outdoor worker who spends six hours a day outside through summer. Here the environmental and clothing layers do most of the work and can be systematic, because the worker controls the routine less than the conditions, and sunscreen is applied to the surfaces that remain exposed and reapplied on a schedule tied to breaks rather than to a memory. Case two: an office worker with a commuting walk and a window desk, as in the example above, where the largest exposure hours are indoors through glass and the design moves the desk and shades the window because no product can be relied on for a whole working day. Case three: a winter skier at altitude, where the ultraviolet index is low but snow reflection and altitude increase exposure, and where the published advice is the same product standard as summer: broad-spectrum, water-resistant, SPF 30 or higher, applied fifteen minutes before exposure and reapplied at least every two hours. Case four: someone who wears a daily tinted product with a low factor because it is the only thing they will apply. Here the correct reasoning is not that the product is useless, but that its labelled value assumes a tested dose that cosmetic application rarely reaches, so the gains available are in dose, reapplication, and the surrounding shade and clothing layers. Case five: a person who tans easily and considers protection unnecessary because they do not burn. The tan is evidence of ultraviolet exposure and of a damage response, not of protection, and people of all skin tones can develop skin cancer, which is why the guidance does not exempt anyone.
depth.mistake: Four errors recur. The first is reading a burn as the exposure meter, which is the error the earlier lesson on wavelengths established: redness is predominantly an ultraviolet B signal, so a day without burning carries no information about ultraviolet A. The second is treating sunscreen as a licence to extend exposure, rather than as one of three measures that reduce dose without eliminating it. The third is seasonal and situational exemption: skipping protection in winter, in the car, under cloud, and on days spent indoors by glass, when the exposure that accumulates in ordinary weeks is larger in hours than a holiday and is dominated by the wavelength that passes through windows. The fourth is missed surfaces and missed timing: ears, nose, lips, back of the neck, and the tops of the hands and feet are commonly skipped, and a single morning application is not maintained through a day, while water resistance is a measured interval in minutes rather than permission for a whole afternoon. Diagnose your own plan with three questions. Which of my weekly hours are outdoors or behind glass, and what do I actually do about them? Which of my exposure surfaces never receives anything? And what is my reapplication trigger, expressed as an event such as two hours of outdoor time, swimming, or heavy sweating, rather than as an intention? Refer any changing, bleeding, itching or non-healing lesion to a clinician, and treat vitamin D concerns and pigmentary conditions as clinical questions rather than reasons to improvise exposure.
depth.application: Nonblocking task with an exposure profile and a written layer plan. Build a table of the exposures that repeat in your week: activity, minutes, whether glass or shade intervenes, time of day, and which surface is exposed. Then add a fourth column naming the layer you will use: environmental, clothing, or product, and specify it. Compute your weekly outdoor and behind-glass hours for the table so the priorities are visible. Model response: 'Weekday walk, 15 minutes twice, direct morning sun, face and hands — environmental: different route with shade; product: about 1.2 grams face and neck applied fifteen minutes before leaving. Drive home, 2 hours, side-window sun, left side of face and neck — clothing: long-sleeved layer and hat; no product relying. Desk, 6 hours, glass — environmental: blind closed on the sunny side. Weekly hours: about 22.5 outdoors or behind glass, so the desk and the drive are the biggest items and neither is burn-producing.' Self-review rubric: (1) hours are computed and the largest exposures are addressed first; (2) at least one layer requires no product and no memory; (3) product use states the surface, the approximate amount, the timing before exposure, and a reapplication trigger; (4) the ears, nose, lips, back of the neck, and backs of the hands are explicitly listed as covered or deliberately uncovered; (5) no risk score is estimated and any changing or non-healing lesion, or any concern about vitamin D or a pigmentary condition, is listed as a clinical question rather than addressed by routine adjustment.
depth.summary: Ordinary days deliver more exposure hours than holidays, and much of that exposure is incidental, indoors, and burn-free because glass transmits ultraviolet A far more readily than ultraviolet B. The reliable plan therefore layers environmental and clothing measures that need no memory on top of correct product use: broad-spectrum SPF 30 or higher, applied at the tested dose roughly fifteen minutes before exposure, reapplied at least every two hours outdoors and after swimming or sweating, with the ears, nose, lips, neck and hands specifically covered. The final lesson takes this whole toolkit, from barrier mechanism to claim structure, and applies it to a single product label and a single marketing claim in a documented audit.

readings.title: American Academy of Dermatology, How to Practice Safe Sun (aad.org) — the three recommendations
readings.note: Read the three recommendations in order: seek shade, noting that the sun's rays are strongest between 10 a.m. and 2 p.m. and that you should seek shade whenever your shadow is shorter than you are; wear sun-protective clothing including a lightweight long-sleeved shirt, pants, a wide-brimmed hat and UV-protective sunglasses, selecting clothing with an ultraviolet protection factor number when possible; and use sunscreen. Also note the framing that everyone is at risk and that skin cancer is one of the most preventable cancers. This is the published basis for the lesson's three-layer design.

readings.title: American Academy of Dermatology, Why you need sun protection in winter (aad.org) — cold-weather protection section
readings.note: Read for the two seasonal points used in this lesson: that clear cold skies still transmit ultraviolet radiation and that risk can increase at altitude and where snow reflects light, and for the specific product directions attributed to the quoted dermatologist — broad-spectrum, water-resistant, SPF 30 or higher, applied at least 15 minutes before exposure and reapplied at least every two hours or after swimming or sweating. The list of commonly missed areas (ears, nose, lips, back of the neck, tops of the hands and feet) also appears here and is the basis for the missed-surfaces check in the application task.

readings.title: American Academy of Dermatology, Sunscreen FAQs (aad.org) — sections on how much to use, how often to reapply, and water resistance
readings.note: Read for the consumer-facing quantities and timing that this lesson refers to: roughly one ounce for the body, at least a teaspoon for the face, reapplication about every two hours or after swimming or sweating, and the statement that no sunscreen may be labelled waterproof or sweatproof. Compare these rounded figures with the dose arithmetic from the tested 2 milligrams per square centimetre and note which surfaces and densities each figure assumes; the numbers are rounded upward deliberately because most people underapply. This page was also used in the earlier level's sunscreen lesson, read for the same quantities, so treat it as a shared reference rather than a new source.

visual.title: The week that matters more than the holiday
visual.description: A panel comparing annual exposure hours from ordinary days against a two-week holiday, with a breakdown of the ordinary week into walking, driving, desk-by-glass and exercise. Below it, a three-layer protection stack draws the environmental, clothing and product measures with the product layer showing dose, timing and reapplication markers, and a missed-surfaces checklist.
steps: Bar 1: ordinary week computed as 15 minutes twice daily for five days, giving about 2.5 hours, plus a 2-hour daily drive at 10 hours, plus 6 hours of desk-by-glass time at 30 hours, plus a 40-minute run.
Bar 2: holiday shown as 2 hours a day for 14 days, about 28 hours, drawn shorter than the commuting hours to make the comparison visible rather than rhetorical.
Spectral inset between the bars: glass pane transmitting ultraviolet A while attenuating ultraviolet B, labelled no burn signal.
Layer 1, environmental: shade symbol with the 10 a.m. to 2 p.m. window and the shadow rule — shadow shorter than you means seek shade.
Layer 2, clothing: long-sleeved light layer, wide-brimmed hat, UV-protective sunglasses and a UPF-numbered garment, labelled protection that needs no reapplication.

Layer 3, product: broad-spectrum, water-resistant, SPF 30 or higher, applied at least 15 minutes before exposure, about 1.2 grams for a 600-square-centimetre face and neck area, with markers for reapplication at two hours, after swimming and after heavy sweating.

Missed-surfaces checklist: ears, nose, lips, back of the neck, tops of the hands and feet, drawn as an outline with unmarked zones; an outdoor-day calculation beside it shows an initial application plus four reapplications for eight hours and roughly 9 grams for face, ears and neck.

lessons.title: Capstone: auditing one label and one claim with the whole toolkit
lessons.explanation: This lesson asks you to do the thing the whole level has been building toward: take one product you actually own, and separate what the law and the test methods establish from what the marketing asserts. Work in four passes. Pass one is the ingredient list, read as a document with rules rather than as a list of heroes. FDA's labelling summary states that cosmetic ingredients must be declared in descending order of predominance, and it also records an exception under which certain ingredients may be declared without regard for predominance, which is why a long tail of named actives at the end of a list tells you very little about how much of each is present. The list is a legitimate way to find out whether a product contains fragrance, a preservative system, or an ingredient you have previously reacted to; it is not a concentration report. Pass two is the regulatory classification. FDA states that cosmetic labelling claims must be truthful and not misleading, that there is no pre-market approval of cosmetics or list of approved claims, and that if a product is marketed with claims for purposes such as treating or preventing disease, or affecting the structure or function of the body including the skin, it is a drug under the law and must meet drug requirements even if it affects appearance. FDA also states that the term cosmeceutical has no meaning under the law, and its separate page on hypoallergenic cosmetics records that no federal standards or definitions govern the term. Pass three is the evidentiary audit of the specific claims, which is where advertising law supplies the discipline: the Federal Trade Commission's health products guidance describes examining the express and implied claims an advertisement conveys and evaluating whether the scientific support is adequate for those claims. The practical instrument is six questions, namely which molecule, at what concentration, in what vehicle, for how long, compared with what, and measured how. Pass four is the routine decision, using the audit sheet, the dose arithmetic and the trial design from earlier lessons. This is education about how to read claims and labels; it is not advice about any medical condition, and nothing here justifies using a cosmetic product in place of clinical care.
lessons.example: Worked example: a full audit of one product and one claim, written as a learner would write it. The product is a serum whose front label says clinically proven, dermatologist tested, pharmaceutical grade, and reduces acne scars, and whose fine print names a retinoid-like active at a stated percentage. Audit the claims one at a time against the four passes. Pharmaceutical grade is not a regulatory category for cosmetics, so it has no defined content. Dermatologist tested describes an activity rather than a result, discloses no protocol, no number of participants, no duration and no comparator, and is not federally defined, so it cannot support a comparison between two products. Cosmeceutical does not appear here but would have the same problem: FDA states the term has no meaning under the law. Clinically proven asserts that evidence exists, and under advertising standards the question is whether adequate substantiation exists for the specific claim conveyed; the test is the six-question instrument, and in this case the label supplies a molecule and a percentage but no vehicle comparison, no duration, no controlled design and no outcome measure, so the claim remains a claim. Reduces acne scars is the consequential one. A scar is a collagen defect that no topical routine rebuilds, and a claim to treat or affect a condition crosses into drug territory, which is why the wording of a claim changes a product's legal category rather than merely its marketing tone. Now do the arithmetic the label never does. If the serum is 30 millilitres and the learner applies about 1.2 grams daily, and the density is near 1 gram per millilitre, the bottle lasts about 25 days, so twelve months of daily use consumes roughly fifteen bottles. That is the real commitment a daily serum represents, and it belongs beside any claim about results. Then close with the routine decision: the product enters only as a substitution for a step whose job it would perform, one variable at a time, with a written observation window and stop rule; and the scar question goes to a clinician.
lessons.question: A serum label claims dermatologist tested, pharmaceutical grade, clinically proven, and reduces acne scars. Which pair of conclusions is most defensible?
lessons.answer: The first two statements have no governing standard, the efficacy claim requires substantiation for the specific claim conveyed, and the scar claim fails on biology while also shifting the product into the drug category
lessons.distractor: All four statements are usable evidence because they appear on a pharmacy product, and the scar claim is the strongest of them because a scar is a visible endpoint a learner can check
lessons.correction: Two phrases have neither regulatory nor test definition, so they cannot support a comparison between products. Clinically proven is an evidence assertion judged against the specific claim conveyed, and the label supplies neither comparator nor duration nor outcome measure. The scar claim fails on biology as well, because acne scars are collagen defects, and a claim to treat or affect a condition also makes the product a drug under FDA's explanation of labelling claims.

depth.definitions: A labelling claim is a statement on a product's labelling; an advertising claim is a statement in advertising, and FDA states that FDA regulates cosmetic labelling while the Federal Trade Commission regulates advertising claims. Cosmetics are products intended for cleansing, beautifying, promoting attractiveness or altering appearance; a product marketed to treat or prevent disease, or to affect the structure or function of the body, is a drug under the law. Substantiation is the evidence an advertiser must hold to support the claims conveyed. INCI names are the standardised ingredient names used in ingredient declarations. Predominance ordering is the requirement that ingredients be declared in descending order of predominance, subject to an exception permitting certain ingredients to be declared without regard for predominance. An adverse event report is a problem reported to a regulator, and FDA provides a consumer route for reporting cosmetic product complaints.
depth.mechanism: The reasoning here is epistemic rather than dermal, and it applies the same structure used throughout this level. A claim is informative when it names a measurable quantity, a defined comparison and a timeframe, because only then could a person check it. Each of the six questions removes one way for a claim to be non-informative without being false: which molecule excludes category words with no standard, at what concentration excludes hero-ingredient storytelling, in what vehicle excludes cross-product percentage comparisons, for how long excludes effects that depend on indefinite use, compared with what excludes uncontrolled testimonials, and measured how excludes visible endpoints assessed by the person selling the product. Inside the product, delivery is the limiting step, which is the substantive reason the six questions matter rather than a rhetorical device: an active must be stable in the formulation, released from it, and able to cross a barrier whose permeability varies, and evidence from a different vehicle does not transfer automatically, a point the vitamin C review made explicitly when it noted that clinical studies of different topical formulations remain limited and that no comparative study establishes an optimal delivery method. One more mechanism belongs to the learner rather than the bottle: irritation is additive across products, so any addition consumes part of a shared budget, which is why the audit ends with a substitution decision rather than a verdict on whether a product is good. The honest limit: some products with weak claim structure still contain well-studied ingredients, and some with excellent claim structure contain a formulation that does not suit a given person. The audit ranks evidence, not products.
depth.secondExample: Contrasting application of the same instrument to a well-formed claim and to a cosmetics-law trap. Claim A, on a sunscreen: broad-spectrum, SPF 30, water-resistant, with instructions to apply about fifteen minutes before exposure and reapply at least every two hours. Run the six questions. The endpoint is defined by the test method, the vehicle is the tested product, the comparison is against unprotected skin, the measurement is erythema-based with a separate ultraviolet A proportionality test for the broad-spectrum claim, and the timeframe is bounded by the reapplication instruction and the water-resistance interval. This claim is informative, which is why it is worth more than most sentences on a serum bottle, and it shows that the audit does not treat all labels as dishonest. Claim B: a product marketed for sensitive skin, described as hypoallergenic and formulated without a named list of ingredients. Here the trap is exclusion logic, because a list can only exclude what it names, FDA records that no federal standards or definitions govern hypoallergenic, and a person's allergen may be a preservative or emulsifier not on the list or may arrive by transfer from a product used elsewhere. Claim C: a product described as registered or approved in some administrative sense. FDA states that cosmetic labelling does not require pre-market approval and that it does not maintain a list of approved claims, so registration language describes paperwork rather than effectiveness. Set A against B and C and the instrument shows its value: it discriminates rather than dismissing everything.
depth.mistake: Three errors dominate. The first is authority transfer, treating a professional-sounding phrase, a pharmacy channel or a medical-looking package as evidence, when the phrase may have no definition and the channel implies nothing about testing. The second is ingredient as conclusion, finding a named active in the list and treating its presence as proof of effect without asking about concentration, vehicle, duration or comparator, and while reading a long tail of actives that may each be present at levels that do not produce the claimed effect. The third is asymmetry with the tool itself: applying forensic scepticism to the product and none to the plan, so that a well-argued market claim replaces a trial design, a dose or a clinical referral. Diagnose your own reasoning by converting each statement into the question it answers, then asking whether that question has a defined measure. If it does, the statement is information; if not, it is positioning. Then check your own plan the same way: does it have a single variable, a window, a dose, an observation and an exit rule, and does it route anything clinical to a clinician? One boundary is absolute: this instrument is for appearances and comfort, so an active disease, a changing lesion, a suspected contact allergy, a suspected infection or a pregnancy-related question is clinician territory regardless of how well any claim is worded.
depth.application: Capstone nonblocking task. Choose one product you own or can read online and produce a one-page audit in five sections. Section one: the ingredient list, quoting the first five ingredients exactly and identifying any fragrance, preservative or previously problematic ingredient, with the note that ordering reflects predominance and that an exception permits certain ingredients to be declared without regard for predominance. Section two: classification, stating whether the wording is appearance-only or makes a drug-type claim, and whether any term used has a governing standard. Section three: the claim table, quoting each efficacy statement exactly, answering the six questions, and marking each statement as informative, plausible but unspecified, or meaningless. Section four: the arithmetic, computing grams per application from the area and the tested dose of 2 milligrams per square centimetre, the days the package lasts, and the cost per month at that dose. Section five: the decision, written as a substitution or a rejection with one reason, plus a trial window, a stop rule and any referral. Model response: section three lists the claim that the product visibly reduces the look of fine lines in eight weeks, then answers the six questions as molecule unspecified, concentration unspecified, vehicle this product, duration eight weeks stated, comparator none, measurement unspecified, giving the classification plausible but unspecified, which means it cannot be checked as written. Section four computes 600 square centimetres at 2 milligrams per square centimetre as 1.2 grams daily, so a 30-millilitre bottle lasts about 25 days and a year consumes roughly fifteen bottles. Section five rejects the product as an addition, proposes it only as a substitution for the serum already in the routine, sets a four-week window, writes a stop rule for persistent burning, swelling or spread, and alters no prescription. Self-review rubric: (1) claims are quoted exactly rather than paraphrased; (2) each classification is justified by what is missing rather than by brand preference; (3) arithmetic shows units and states the area and density assumptions; (4) the decision is a substitution with a window, a stop rule and a named clinical contact for anything serious; (5) no diagnosis is offered, no product is described as treating a disease, and no prescribed treatment is changed. If you cannot answer the six questions for your own product from the available information, that is itself the finding.
depth.summary: One label, one claim, four passes: what the ingredients legally tell you and do not, what the wording makes the product in regulatory terms, what the six questions reveal about each efficacy statement, and what the arithmetic and the trial design say about using it. The instrument discriminates between informative and uninformative claims rather than dismissing all marketing, and it applies to your own plan as strictly as to the bottle. Level five ends where the whole course began: mechanism first, dose and context second, honest expectations third, and a clear line where cosmetic care hands over to clinical care.

readings.title: U.S. Food and Drug Administration, Cosmetics Labeling Claims (fda.gov) — the opening statements on truthfulness, drug classification, and the FTC division of labour
readings.note: Read the first four paragraphs for the exact framing this lesson uses: cosmetic labelling claims must be truthful and not misleading, FDA does not approve claims before market and has no list of approved claims, claims to treat or prevent disease or to affect the structure or function of the body make a product a drug that must meet drug requirements, and FDA regulates labelling claims while the FTC regulates advertising claims. Then follow the label-claims links to the hypoallergenic and cosmeceutical pages, the two terms an audit most often has to test.

readings.title: U.S. Food and Drug Administration, Summary of Cosmetics Labeling Requirements (fda.gov) — the ingredients section
readings.note: Read the ingredient declaration material for the statement that ingredients must be declared in descending order of predominance, and for the recorded exception permitting certain ingredients to be declared without regard for predominance. That exception is the basis for this lesson's warning that a long tail of named actives conveys little about how much of each is present. Use the page as the reference that makes an ingredient list a governed document rather than marketing copy.

readings.title: U.S. Food and Drug Administration, the page for the term cosmeceutical (fda.gov) — the short statement
readings.note: Read the brief passage stating that the term has no meaning under the law and that industry uses it for products with drug-like benefits while the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act does not recognise it. Use it whenever a product's apparent authority rests on that word, and notice how short the page is: there is no definition to research because none exists. This page was also used in the previous level; here it is applied inside a full label audit.

readings.title: Federal Trade Commission, Health Products Compliance Guidance (ftc.gov) — Section I Preface and Section II Overview of Regulatory Framework
readings.note: Read the Preface for the description of the guidance as covering how claims about benefits and safety must be truthful, not misleading and supported by science, and for the point that the same legal principles apply to the marketing of any health-related product. Read Section II for the Commission's authority over advertising and for how express and implied claims are identified. It is written for advertisers, which is exactly why it is useful to a learner: it states what a claim must be able to support. The document itself says it is staff guidance without the force of law and provides no safe harbour.

visual.title: The four-pass audit and the six-question claim test
visual.description: A one-page audit form drawn as four stacked passes around a product in the centre. Pass one shows the ingredient list with an ordering arrow and an exception note. Pass two is a classification gate labelled appearance-only versus drug-type claim. Pass three is a table of claims each run through six question boxes. Pass four is a dose and cost calculation feeding a substitution decision with a trial window and a stop rule.
steps: Pass 1: ingredient list with a descending arrow labelled predominance, the first five ingredients highlighted, and a note that an exception permits certain ingredients to be declared without regard for predominance, so the tail of the list is uninformative about amount.
Pass 1 side checks: mark any fragrance, preservative system or previously reacted ingredient, with the purpose stated as exposure mapping rather than efficacy ranking.

Pass 2: classification gate with a left branch labelled appearance-only claim and a right branch labelled treats or prevents disease or affects structure or function, the right branch carrying the note that this makes the product a drug requiring drug-level evidence.
Pass 2 term strip: cosmeceutical marked no meaning under the law; hypoallergenic marked no federal standard or definition; pharmaceutical grade and dermatologist tested marked no governing standard.
Pass 3: claim table with one row per quoted statement and six columns for molecule, concentration, vehicle, duration, comparator and measurement, each cell either filled or marked missing.

Pass 3 classification row: informative when measurable quantities, a comparison and a timeframe are present; plausible but unspecified when some are missing; meaningless when the wording has no defined reference.

Pass 4: dose box computing grams per application as area times 2 milligrams per square centimetre, then days per package and cost per month, feeding a decision box labelled substitute, reject or trial.

Pass 4 gate: one variable, a stated window, a written stop rule for persistent burning, swelling or spread, and a referral arrow for active disease, a changing lesion, suspected contact allergy, suspected infection, or any pregnancy-related question.

questions.prompt: A learner has flat brown marks from old lesions, generalised redness that fades when they lie down, and shallow oval depressions, and asks which product will remove the depressions. What are the components and the honest ceiling for each?
questions.answer: Pigment clears slowly with turnover, redness is vascular and resolves on its own schedule, and the depressions are a collagen defect no topical routine rebuilds, so complete resolution of scarring is the exception rather than the rule
questions.distractor: All three are pigment at different depths, so a longer course of a stronger lightening product will resolve the marks, the redness and the depressions together
questions.correction: Three tissues are involved. Melanin clears as keratinocytes are shed, microvascular dilatation produces redness that is not pigment, and depressions come from net collagen loss or fibrous tethering that a cream cannot fill. The scar literature reports that most acne scars are atrophic from collagen destruction and states that complete resolution of acne scarring is the exception rather than the rule, so a topical plan should promise nothing about the depression.

questions.prompt: A learner with scalp itching, flaking, a rash at the hairline and behind the ears, and frequent breakage asks whether a stronger medicated shampoo and a protein treatment are the right purchases. Which reading is most defensible?
questions.answer: The scalp reaction is a product-exposure question needing assessment with the products available, and the breakage reflects cumulative cuticle loss and mechanical stress, so the next moves are an exposure map and a handling audit
questions.distractor: Both purchases are appropriate, because scalp flaking indicates a hygiene or fungal problem that medicated shampoo resolves while protein fills the gaps left by breakage
questions.correction: Scalp scaling has several possible causes, and hairline and eyelid involvement points to a contact reaction rather than poor hygiene, with shampoos recognised as allergen sources including betaine surfactants and preservatives. Breakage follows weathering: wet hair tolerates about 30 percent extension, changes irreversibly between about 30 and 70 percent and fractures near 80, so technique and heat matter as much as products. Naming a cause is a clinician's job.

questions.prompt: Using the tested dose of 2 milligrams per square centimetre, how much moisturiser does a learner with two hands of about 360 square centimetres need per application and across a twelve-week winter at twice daily?
questions.answer: About 0.72 grams per application and roughly 121 grams over twelve weeks, which is more than a 100-gram tube
questions.distractor: About 0.07 grams per application and roughly 12 grams over twelve weeks, so one small tube comfortably covers the season
questions.correction: 360 square centimetres times 2 milligrams per square centimetre is 720 milligrams, or 0.72 grams, and twice daily for 84 days gives about 121 grams. The distractor is a factor of ten low and would leave the film too thin to act, which is how learners wrongly conclude that a moisturiser does not work.

questions.prompt: A learner applies broad-spectrum SPF 50 once each morning, drives two hours daily with sun through the side window, sits six hours by glass, never burns, and asks whether the factor should be raised. What does the reasoning conclude?
questions.answer: The unburning exposure is largely ultraviolet A through glass, one application is not maintained at the tested dose through a day, and the largest gains come from shade, clothing and reapplication rather than a higher printed factor
questions.distractor: The factor should be raised, because not burning shows the product works and a higher number would extend that protection across the whole day
questions.correction: Erythema is a predominantly ultraviolet B response, and glass attenuates ultraviolet B far more than ultraviolet A, so a long burn-free drive can still deliver meaningful ultraviolet A. The labelled value assumes 2 milligrams per square centimetre, which a single morning application does not maintain. Ordinary weeks also accumulate more exposure hours than a holiday, so the environmental and clothing layers matter more than the number on the bottle.

questions.prompt: A serum is described as pharmaceutical grade, dermatologist tested, clinically proven, and formulated for sensitive skin, and claims to reduce acne scars. Which audit conclusion is most defensible?
questions.answer: Two phrases have no governing standard, the efficacy statement needs substantiation for the specific claim conveyed, and the scar claim fails on biology while also shifting the product into the drug category
questions.distractor: Four of the five statements are usable evidence because they describe professional involvement, and the scar claim is acceptable because acne scars are a visible surface problem
questions.correction: Pharmaceutical grade is not a regulatory category for cosmetics and dermatologist tested describes an activity rather than a result, so neither supports comparison. Clinically proven is an evidence assertion judged against the specific claim conveyed, and the label supplies no comparator, duration or outcome measure. Scars are collagen defects rather than surface problems, and claims to affect a condition also make a product a drug under FDA's labelling claims explanation.

questions.prompt: A learner brings a routine of eleven steps, reports stinging on three of them, wants to test a new niacinamide serum, a new azelaic product and a weekly peel in the same month, and says their face has never felt fully calm. Using the audit and attribution logic from this level, explain the order of operations, what must be removed before anything is added, and what the test design has to contain.
questions.answer: Collapse the duplicated jobs and subtract the stripping steps to reach a tolerated baseline, list the three candidates in order of the job each would actually fill, then introduce one variable at a time with a stated window, an observable endpoint and a written stop rule before any clinician-referred question is addressed
questions.distractor: Run all three new products in parallel for a month because they act on different mechanisms, then evaluate the routine as a whole and remove whichever step seems least useful afterwards
questions.correction: Nothing in this level can be evaluated on an unstable baseline, and stinging on existing steps means the insult is already too high, so removal comes first and the retained steps are those that each perform a job no other step performs. The three candidates are then ranked by whether the routine actually needs that job, because a niacinamide serum, an azelaic product and a peel overlap with steps the learner may already have. Testing them together forfeits attribution, since several simultaneous changes cannot be assigned outcomes, whereas sequential trials give one candidate explanation per window. The design also needs the observation to be checkable and the exit rule to be written before starting, with a named clinical contact for anything serious.

questions.prompt: A learner intends to use twenty percent niacinamide every morning, a twenty-five percent vitamin C serum every evening, a ten percent glycolic acid four nights a week and a prescription-strength azelaic product from a relative, all while reporting that their skin has become reactive. Evaluate the plan using the reported concentration ranges, the formulation differences and the shared irritation budget.
questions.answer: The concentrations exceed the ranges the cited reviews report as useful, azelaic products differ by vehicle more than by percentage so the borrowed product cannot be assessed from its label, and four overlapping commitments draw on one barrier, so the plan should be reduced to one tolerated active introduced into a stable routine with no borrowed prescription involved
questions.distractor: The plan is defensible because the four products target pigmentation, oxidation, desquamation and inflammation respectively, and using them at different times of day keeps the mechanisms independent
questions.correction: Niacinamide is reported in sebum studies at two to five percent with tolerance documented to five and no stinging to ten, and vitamin C needs above roughly eight percent with nothing gained above twenty, so the chosen strengths add exposure without documented benefit. Azelaic acid's absorbed fraction differs sharply between the gel and cream formulations, so a percentage on one product says nothing about another. Time-of-day separation does not separate mechanisms, because every one of these steps perturbs the same stratum corneum, and irritation is additive across the week. A product obtained from another person is also outside any plan a clinician set.

questions.prompt: Two weeks after stopping an acid, a toner and a retinoid, a learner's stinging has resolved and they want to restart the acid immediately, then add a stronger one next week because the first felt fine. Their retinoid is a prescription product. Explain what the repair timeline says about this plan, what evidence should precede any reintroduction, and what must not be decided by the learner.
questions.answer: Symptom resolution precedes restoration of permeability, so a deliberate hold with two consecutive stable weeks comes before a single reintroduction, the reintroduction follows the trial design with one variable and a stop rule, and the prescription's timing and resumption belong to the prescriber
questions.distractor: Resolution of stinging means the barrier is restored, so restarting the acid immediately is appropriate and adding a stronger one a week later simply tests tolerance faster
questions.correction: The two curves in the repair model move at different speeds: inflammation settles within days while intercellular lipid organisation, corneocyte cohesion and irritant thresholds take weeks, so feeling recovered is not being recovered and early resumption lands new exposure on a still-permeable surface. That is why a hold with two consecutive stable observations is the precondition for testing, and why the reintroduction itself has to be a single-variable trial with an observable endpoint. A prescribed retinoid is not the learner's variable to restart on a whim, because the schedule and the decision to resume sit with the prescriber.

questions.prompt: A learner has mixed findings on both cheeks: flat brown patches, generalised redness, and several shallow oval depressions, plus two new tender lesions they have been squeezing. They ask which serum will resolve everything before a wedding in eight weeks. Explain the components, the driver, the timescales and the expectations, and state what the eight-week deadline cannot change.
questions.answer: Pigment clears over months with turnover, redness is vascular and resolves on its own schedule, depressions are a collagen defect no topical routine rebuilds, and squeezing renews the inflammatory driver that produces pigment, so the plan is to stop manipulating lesions, protect from ultraviolet exposure, seek clinical assessment for the active lesions and the textural component, and state that the deadline does not compress the biology
questions.distractor: A single high-strength lightening and exfoliating serum will address all three components within eight weeks if applied twice daily, because pigment, redness and textural loss all respond to accelerated cell turnover
questions.correction: Three tissues require three different answers and only one of them is visible at the surface. Melanin clears with epidermal turnover over months and dermal pigment longer, vascular redness is not pigment at all, and depressions follow net collagen loss or fibrous tethering, which no cream can fill. The reported finding that complete resolution of acne scarring is the exception rather than the rule is the honest expectation to set. Squeezing renews both inflammation and pigment, so the driver has to stop, and exfoliating pigmented skin is a documented route to new pigment. A fixed eight-week date can organise the plan but cannot change the timescales.

questions.prompt: A learner reports four facts: an itchy scaly rash at the hairline and on both eyelids, frequent short broken hairs, a new shampoo and leave-in treatment started ten days ago, and daily blow-drying with tight styles worn five days a week. Sort these into mechanisms, state what the exposure map and the fibre mechanics each explain, and identify what must go to a clinician.
questions.answer: The rash pattern with eyelid involvement points to a contact reaction requiring clinical assessment with the products available, since a leave-on product at the hairline and transfer from the hands can reach the eyelids, while breakage follows cumulative cuticle loss, water uptake and mechanical and thermal stress that the handling log quantifies
questions.distractor: The rash is a scalp hygiene problem resolvable with a stronger medicated shampoo, and the breakage is caused by the shampoo being applied to the length rather than the scalp, so changing application alone resolves both
questions.correction: Rinse-off and leave-on exposures behave differently, because a leave-on product has a longer contact time at exactly the symptomatic margin, and the published allergen list for shampoos includes betaine surfactants, preservatives and fragrance components, so a hygiene explanation is not supported and the substance cannot be named from appearance. Fibre damage accumulates through cuticle lifting, loss of the surface lipid layer, water uptake and swelling, and then fracture; wet hair tolerates about 30 percent extension, changes irreversibly between about 30 and 70, and fractures near 80, so wet brushing, towel rubbing, heat passes and sustained pulling are counted events. Persistent scalp rash, painful lesions, hair loss or scaling that does not improve after simplification are clinical questions.

questions.prompt: A learner whose hands crack every winter works shifts with many hand washes, wears gloves for long stretches including wet tasks, and applies a pea-sized amount of an expensive hand cream three times a day. Using the dose arithmetic, the site argument and the wet-work evidence, explain why the current approach fails and what the corrected plan contains.
questions.answer: The pea-sized dose leaves the film far below the tested benchmark for an area of about 360 square centimetres needing roughly 0.72 grams per application, repeated wetting and drying plus glove occlusion drives the damage, so the plan is to compute and sustain an adequate dose of a fragrance-free leave-on product after every wash, reduce unnecessary water contact, and choose gloves by task with drying between periods
questions.distractor: The hand cream is too weak, so the correct change is to switch to a stronger active hand product applied the same three times a day while keeping the gloves on for longer to lock in moisture
questions.correction: Area times dose gives the amount: 360 square centimetres at 2 milligrams per square centimetre is 0.72 grams, and twice daily for twelve weeks is about 121 grams, so a small facial-sized product at a pea-sized dose never reaches the effective amount. The occupational literature identifies contact dermatitis as the most common occupational skin disease with wet work as a main risk factor, so repeated washing and drying is the operative exposure, and occlusion over damp skin softens the surface and raises permeability rather than locking moisture in. Persistent hand rash also has irritant, allergic and endogenous forms that appearance cannot separate, so a stronger product is the wrong direction.

questions.prompt: A learner describes their protection as a single morning application of a broad-spectrum SPF 30 product, notes that they never burn, and lists a fifteen-minute walk twice daily, a two-hour afternoon drive with sun through the side window, six hours a day at a desk by glass, and a fortnight's holiday each summer. Construct the exposure argument, the dose argument and the layering argument, and state what the holiday does not justify.
questions.answer: Ordinary weeks accumulate more exposure hours than the holiday, the drive and desk exposures are ultraviolet A rich because glass transmits it far more readily than ultraviolet B, the single morning application is not maintained at the tested dose through a day, so the plan layers shade and clothing first and adds correct product use with measured dose and a reapplication trigger, while the holiday does not justify deferring protection to two weeks a year
questions.distractor: Because the learner never burns, the single morning application is demonstrably sufficient for the daily pattern, so the only change needed is packing a higher-factor product for the summer holiday
questions.correction: Erythema is predominantly an ultraviolet B signal and glass attenuates ultraviolet B much more than ultraviolet A, so an unburning drive and desk exposure can still deliver meaningful dose of the wavelength associated with pigment change, photoaging and immunosuppression. Computing hours makes the point quantitative: about 2.5 hours of walks plus 10 hours of driving plus 30 hours of desk-by-glass time dwarfs a 28-hour holiday. The labelled value assumes 2 milligrams per square centimetre, so dose and reapplication, plus shade and clothing that need no memory, are where the real gains are. Seasonal thinking inverts the priority rather than removing it, since winter skies still transmit ultraviolet radiation and altitude and snow reflection increase exposure.

questions.prompt: Audit this claim set from a product page: cosmetic facility registration, clinically proven to reduce wrinkles, pharmaceutical grade at two percent, oil-free and non-comedogenic, and dermatologist tested. Also explain how the arithmetic of daily use changes the decision, given a 30-millilitre bottle applied at about 1.2 grams a day.
questions.answer: Only claims tied to a defined measure or regulatory category can function as information, so the wrinkle claim needs substantiation for the specific claim conveyed and would make the product a drug if it asserts effect on structure or function, while registration, pharmaceutical grade, non-comedogenic and dermatologist tested have no governing comparative standard, and the dose arithmetic shows the bottle lasts about 25 days, which converts the claim into a commitment of roughly fifteen bottles a year
questions.distractor: Registration and dermatologist testing together establish that the product has been independently verified, so the wrinkle claim can be accepted and the two percent concentration makes the cost per year unimportant
questions.correction: Sort by whether a standard exists. FDA explains that cosmetic labelling does not require pre-market approval and that it maintains no list of approved claims, so registration is administrative. Pharmaceutical grade is not a regulatory category for cosmetics, and non-comedogenic and dermatologist tested are manufacturer assertions without a shared protocol, so none of them supports a comparison between products. A claim to affect the structure or function of the body, or to treat disease, makes a product a drug under the law and requires drug-level evidence. The arithmetic is the part the page never supplies: 30 millilitres at 1.2 grams per day lasts about 25 days, so a year consumes roughly fifteen bottles, which is the real cost of the claim.

questions.prompt: Over one week a learner reports four things: hands that crack and itch after shifts with heavy wet work, stinging on the face after adding a fifth step to a stable routine, a scaly itchy patch at the hairline, and a plan to fix all three by buying a stronger product for each. Prioritise the problems, state the mechanism-based first action for each, and identify which one needs clinical assessment rather than a product change.
questions.answer: Subtract and stabilise the face routine first because the stinging is a tolerance signal about total insult, address the hands by reducing water contact and sustaining an adequate dose of a fragrance-free leave-on product after every wash, map hair-product exposures for the scalp patch, and send the persistent hand problem and the non-improving scalp rash for clinical assessment rather than escalating products
questions.distractor: Buy three stronger products at once, one per site, because each problem is on different skin and stronger formulations address each in isolation without interacting
questions.correction: The three problems have three different mechanisms and one shared error. On the face, stinging after an addition is evidence that the irritation budget is exceeded, so removal and stability come before any evaluation. On the hands, the reviewed occupational data identify wet work as a main risk factor, so the fix is sequence, dose and reduced water contact rather than potency, and a persistent hand rash has irritant, allergic and endogenous forms that appearance cannot separate. At the hairline, contact reactions and treatable scalp conditions look alike and the substance cannot be named from appearance. Site separation does not make exposures independent, because the same person's habits and products link the sites, and escalating three products simultaneously would remove attribution everywhere.

questions.prompt: A learner wants a plan that will, in their words, get rid of their acne scars, fix their melasma, clear their scalp dandruff and stop their hands from cracking, using one strong serum for everything and no clinician visits. Rewrite the request as four separate problems with their correct owners, and state the honest expectation for each.
questions.answer: Scars are a collagen defect needing clinical procedure assessment with complete resolution being the exception rather than the rule, a pigmentation disorder such as melasma is a relapsing clinical condition requiring clinician direction, scalp scaling has several possible causes needing assessment, and hand cracking is driven by wet work and dose and can improve with sustained non-irritating care while persistent dermatitis is clinical, so no single serum addresses any of these and each has a different owner
questions.distractor: One strong multi-active serum can serve all four because the mechanisms overlap: surface renewal improves scars and pigment, sebum control resolves scalp scaling, and lipid ingredients repair the hands
questions.correction: The four requests differ in tissue, driver and ceiling. Pigment and textural change are not the same defect, and textural change is structural, which is why the scar literature states that complete resolution of acne scarring is the exception rather than the rule. Pigmentation disorders have a relapsing course and prescription options, which are clinician territory, particularly in pregnancy or breastfeeding. Scalp scaling can be an inflammatory condition, an irritant reaction or the consequence of a product, and appearance cannot separate them. Hand cracking is driven by cumulative wetting and drying and by dose, so a leave-on product applied at an adequate amount after every wash is the mechanism-based move, with persistent dermatitis referred. Collapsing them into one product also ignores the shared irritation budget that makes each site worse at the same time.

questions.prompt: A learner asks for a single routine that will be stable, then wants to know how to know if it is working, how to add the next step, when to stop, and when to hand over to a clinician. Write the answer as an ordered sequence of decisions with the criteria at each step, drawing on the whole level.
questions.answer: Establish the tolerated baseline by collapsing duplicated jobs and doing one alteration at a time, define the observation and the stop rule before making any change, add a step only as a substitution with one variable and a stated window, hold when observations are stable rather than escalating, and hand over for active disease, a changing lesion, suspected allergy or infection, pregnancy-related questions, or any problem that persists or worsens despite subtraction
questions.distractor: Escalate the strongest available active whenever progress is slower than expected, since visible improvement is the signal that the routine is working and a plateau means the current strength has become insufficient
questions.correction: The sequence is a dependency chain rather than a preference list. A baseline of steps that each perform a distinct job and survive an ordinary week is what makes an outcome attributable, so it comes before any addition, and single-variable changes with a pre-written observation and exit rule are what convert an experience into information. Substitution rather than addition respects the shared irritation budget, and holding at stability rather than escalating is the response that a plateau actually calls for, because many endpoints move on the scale of weeks to months and escalation trades tolerance for nothing measured. Referral triggers close the sequence, because the toolkit governs appearance and comfort only.

questions.prompt: A learner brings a product page with five statements, a routine with nine steps, a scalp that itches, hands that crack, a scar they want gone, and a holiday two weeks away. Produce the integrated plan: what you audit first and how, what you subtract, what you keep, what you protect, and what you hand to a clinician, with the reasoning stated at each point.
questions.answer: Audit the label first by classifying each statement against a defined standard and quoting the efficacy claims exactly, then reduce the routine to steps that each perform a distinct job while protecting from ultraviolet exposure daily rather than seasonally, address scalp and hand problems as exposure and dose questions with clinical assessment where the pattern or persistence warrants it, and accept that a structural scar is not a topical endpoint, so the holiday changes nothing about the plan's order
questions.distractor: Start with the strongest product for the scar because it is the most visible goal, add the remaining steps to a longer routine so each product can act independently, and protect from the sun only during the holiday when exposure is highest
questions.correction: The audit comes first because it determines what any product can even claim, and statements with no governing standard cannot guide a decision: FDA explains that cosmetic labelling requires no pre-market approval, that claims must be truthful and not misleading, and that a claim to affect the structure or function of the body makes a product a drug, while terms such as cosmeceutical, hypoallergenic, pharmaceutical grade and dermatologist tested carry no shared comparative standard. Reduction follows, because every retained step should perform a job no other step performs, and irritation across steps is additive. Protection is a daily habit whose hours in ordinary weeks exceed a holiday, and the holiday itself is incidental exposure that changes nothing structural. Scalp itching and hand cracking are exposure-pattern questions first, with clinical referral where the pattern is delayed or spreading, where the problem persists despite subtraction, or where hair loss or persistent dermatitis appears. A scar is a collagen defect, so the honest expectation is the ceiling.
